items.title: 10.17.3 Oxidising and reducing agents using E standard values

blocks.text: Look back at Figure 10.11. In the list of reduction half-equations, as E standard becomes more negative, the species on the left become weaker oxidising agents (they accept electrons less readily) and the species on the right become stronger reducing agents (they release electrons more readily). Copper will not reduce Zn2+ ions to Zn; to reduce Zn2+ ions a stronger reducing agent is needed, with an E standard more negative than that of Zn2+/Zn. In Figure 10.13 we see that the half-equation Mg2+/Mg has a more negative value, so magnesium is a suitable reducing agent: Zn2+ + e- giving Zn, -0.76 V, and Mg2+ + 2e- giving Mg, -2.38 V. Zn2+ is the better oxidising agent, more likely to accept electrons than Mg2+; Mg is the better reducing agent, more likely to release electrons than Zn.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book writes Zn2+ + e- giving Zn; two electrons are needed: Zn2+ + 2e- giving Zn, E standard = -0.76 V. The list of E standard values referred to as Figure 10.11 and Figure 10.13 is Figure 10.9 (Figure 10.11 is the Nernst graph and there is no Figure 10.13).

Compounds also act as oxidising and reducing agents: KMnO4 (+0.54 V) and K2Cr2O7 (+1.33 V) are oxidising agents because of their high E standard values, whereas KI and FeSO4 are reducing agents because of their low values. A few compounds such as H2O2 act as both oxidising and reducing agents.
With E standard Ag+/Ag +0.80 V, Cr2+/Cr -0.91 V and Fe2+/Fe -0.44 V, which ion is the strongest oxidising agent and which the least, and arrange Ag, Cr and Fe in increasing reducing power.
